hints: Focus on what controls the speed of an SN1 reaction, the slow formation of the carbocation in the first step.
Compare the carbon skeletons first, a halogen on a tertiary carbon gives a much more stable carbocation than on a primary carbon.
Now compare the leaving groups for the two tertiary halides, remembering that iodide leaves far more easily than chloride to speed up that slow step.
walkthrough:
**Recall the SN1 rate-determining step**

Think of SN1 as slow then fast. The slow, rate-determining step is loss of the halide to form a carbocation.

$$\text{R-X} \rightarrow \text{R}^{+} + \text{X}^{-} \text{ (slow)}$$

**Decode the names to primary vs tertiary**

Methylpropane is a 4-carbon branched chain. 1-halo means the halogen is on an end $\text{CH}_{2}\text{X}$ group, so primary. 2-halo means it is on the central carbon, so tertiary.

$$\text{1-halo-2-methylpropane: } (\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{X (primary)}$$ $$\text{2-halo-2-methylpropane: } (\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CX (tertiary)}$$

**Apply carbocation stability**

A tertiary carbocation is stabilised by more inductive electron donation and hyperconjugation from three alkyl groups. A primary carbocation is much less stable and forms very slowly.

$$\text{rate: tertiary } >> \text{ primary}$$

**Apply leaving group ability**

For the two tertiary compounds left, the $\text{C-I}$ bond is longer and weaker than $\text{C-Cl}$, and $\text{I}^{-}$ is a larger, more stable ion than $\text{Cl}^{-}$. So the iodo compound ionises fastest and gives the fastest precipitate of silver halide with $\text{AgNO}_{3}$.

options.A: This is a primary chloride, $(CH3)2CHCH2Cl$. It would form an unstable primary carbocation and has a poor leaving group, so SN1 is extremely slow.
options.B: This is a tertiary chloride, $(CH3)3CCl$. The tertiary carbocation is good for SN1, but chloride is a much poorer leaving group than iodide, so it is slower than the tertiary iodide.
options.C: This is a primary iodide, $(CH3)2CHCH2I$. Iodide is an excellent leaving group, but the primary carbocation is too unstable for fast SN1, so it reacts mainly by SN2, not rapid SN1.
options.D: This is a tertiary iodide, $(CH3)3CI$. It combines both rate-boosting factors: a stable tertiary carbocation and the best leaving group, iodide. It therefore ionises most rapidly in the SN1 slow step.
